extracted.intended_audience: WIPO/statistics users, patent office analysts, IP policymakers, researchers and IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and use of WIPO patent statistics: definitions, measurement conventions, and quality-relevant indicators (e.g., patent families, examination outcomes, patents in force, utility models) used for cross-country comparison and policy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family is a set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention. Patent applications within a family are interlinked by one or more of the following: priority claim, Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists explicitly the linking mechanisms that define family membership; useful for constructing family-based indicators of the same invention filed across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family size as indicator of geographical coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a patent family (indicating the number of offices at which a patent is filed) reflects its geographical coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger family size implies wider geographic protection. Family size is used as a proxy for an invention's geographical reach and (implicitly) its commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A special subset comprises foreign-oriented patent families – that is, those patent families that have at least one filing office different from the office of the applicant’s country of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that some foreign-oriented families include only one filing office if applicants file directly at a foreign office (example: a Canadian applicant filing directly with the USPTO). This definition affects cross-country counts and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent families as quality/value indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-oriented patent families are usually considered to be of higher quality and value. Filing patents in multiple jurisdictions is costly and time-consuming, so applicants tend to be selective about filing outside their domestic jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because foreign-oriented families reduce bias toward domestic filings, they are viewed as more reliable for cross-country comparison and as an indicator of inventions with higher expected economic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (claims assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent offices must assess whether the claims presented in an application meet the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability defined in national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three substantive standards (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability/usefulness) are the core legal thresholds for grant across jurisdictions; differences in national law and examination practice affect grant/rejection rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcomes categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination outcomes are categorized as granted, rejected or withdrawn (including abandoned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics report the distribution of these outcome categories by office and year. Caveat: 'rejection of an application does not mean final rejection' (i.e., prosecution may continue or appeals may follow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-office comparability caveat (examination capacity & procedural delays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between offices in the number of patents granted depends on factors such as examination capacity and procedural delays. For this reason, application data for a given year should not be compared with grant data from the same year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing offices or years, adjust for procedural differences, pendency lags, and data availability (e.g., China 2017 methodological break). Use consistent definitions and consider requests-for-examination policies that delay substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications pending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications pending is defined as all patent applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by a patent office, including those applications for which applicants have not filed a request for examination (where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inclusive definition means pending counts may include large shares of applications that have not yet reached substantive examination in offices with deferred-examination systems; interpret pending stocks accordingly (example: ~80% of pending in Republic of Korea await request for substantive examination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent rights duration and maintenance/renewal requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights generally last for up to 20 years from the date an application is filed. A holder must pay a maintenance/renewal fee in order for a patent to remain valid, and may opt to let a patent lapse before the end of its full term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical indicators include share of patents remaining in force at least 10 years after filing (~36.2% across offices reporting) and share lasting the full 20‑year term (~17.5%). Maintenance fees and lapsing behavior affect 'patents in force' counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents in force (resident vs non-resident composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in force are measured across jurisdictions and broken down by whether the patent was granted to a resident or non-resident applicant. The source composition of patents in force varies considerably between offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High non-resident shares (e.g., UK, France, Germany, Switzerland) versus high resident shares (e.g., China, Japan) reflect national markets and grant patterns; use resident/non-resident splits to interpret domestic vs foreign-derived patent stocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model (UM) definition and comparability notes
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model (UM) is a special form of patent right granted by a state or jurisdiction to an inventor or the inventor’s assignee for a fixed period of time. The terms and conditions for granting a UM differ slightly from those for normal patents, including a shorter term of protection and less stringent eligibility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UM statistics are typically reported separately; UM filings are overwhelmingly resident in many jurisdictions (China accounts for ~98% of global UMs in 2023). UM vs patent filing patterns vary by country and income level — treat them as distinct rights when comparing innovation activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor participation metrics (gender participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation of women inventors is measured as the share of women among listed inventors in published PCT applications and the share of published PCT applications naming at least one woman as inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these metrics to evaluate diversity trends (example: women constituted 17.7% of all inventors listed in published PCT applications in 2023; share with at least one woman rose from 21.4% in 2009 to 36.2% in 2023). Field- and country-level variation should be considered.
